# (2026-08-17)

## ⭐⭐⭐ AW CARRIES THE COMPLETE CoD TYPE LIBRARY: 11,434 STRUCTS

The single most valuable artifact found for the documentation-first goal. AW's
IDB has 18,531 type ordinals, 11,434 UDTs, 1,169 of them over 500 bytes -- the
whole engine type set, with real field names:

    clientDemoPlayback_t   6,228,892   what this file calls "PlaybackData"
    serverStatic_t         2,182,272
    cg_s / cg_t              789,248   "cg"
    clientStatic_t           759,296   "cls"
    client_t                 465,280
    clientConnection_t       418,416   "clc"
    server_t                 285,252
    snapshot_s               109,184
    clientDemoMain_t          85,224
    playerState_s             14,848   "ps"        166 members
    WeaponDef                  2,792               582 members
    gentity_s                    640
    centity_s                    524
    entityState_s                256    30 members
    LerpEntityState / cpose_t    108
    pmove_t / pml_t          396 / 300   the MOVEMENT code
    msg_t                         48

**Every raw offset this project derived by hand has a NAME waiting there.**
Captured to `re/aw_engine_types.json` (34 core types with full member lists) and
`re/aw_entity_types.json`.

### ⚠ NAMES AND STRUCTURE TRANSFER. OFFSETS DO NOT.

AW is 32-bit PPC and five years older. Its centity_s is 524 bytes against S2's
1808; entityState_s agrees at `number`@0 and `otherEntityNum`@2 and then diverges
immediately (AW eType@0xc, S2 eType at +10 relative). Use AW as a TEMPLATE to map
against, never as offsets to copy.

### PROVEN TRUSTWORTHY — the msg_t control

S2's msg_t layout was derived independently months ago from MSG_Init/MSG_BeginReading.
Every single field matches AW's names, and AW resolves the two left UNKNOWN:

    AW off  AW name            S2 off  what this file had recorded
    +0      overflowed         +0      "cleared on BeginReading [overflow-ish]"
    +4      readOnly           +4      "set to 1 by Init [UNKNOWN]"      <- RESOLVED
    +8      data               +8      data pointer (PROVEN)
    +12     splitData          +16     "second data pointer [split data?]"
    +16/+20 maxsize/cursize    +24/+28 size/size
    +24     splitSize          +32     "0 on Init"                       <- RESOLVED
    +28/+32 readcount/bit      +36/+40 read cursor / bit position
    +36     lastEntityRef      +44     msg+44, the 4780 delta index
    +44     useZlib            +52     useZlib

`clientDemoPlayback_t` corroborates just as hard: `+8 completed`, `+24
totalBytesRead` ("the money field"), `+28 timeScale` (proven here from the arrow
keys), and **keyFrame[250] at 12,000 bytes = 48 bytes/slot** -- exactly the
250-slot 48-byte keyframe ring documented from S2's own ProcessKeyFrameJump.

## ⭐⭐ S2 centity_s — MAPPED FROM S2'S OWN CODE

Before today "centity" was ~8 scattered offsets from the nametag work, several
unverified. `re/map_centity.py` now derives them properly: CG_GetEntity returns a
centity*, so every dereference of its return value in all **306 callers** is a
field access. Decompile each, track the variable, collect every
`*(TYPE *)(var + N)`.

    116 distinct field offsets, from 306 functions.
    Highest offset touched is +1804 -- fitting EXACTLY inside the 1808 stride,
    which independently confirms the stride.

### Region map (evidence-derived)

    0    .. 1168   pose (cpose_t) + prevState (LerpEntityState)
                   OWORD run at 1048/1064/1080/1096/1112/1128/1144 (16-byte
                   spaced) = trajectory vectors
    1168 .. 1696   nextState (entityState_s)  -> ~528 bytes vs AW's 256
      1340         nextState.lerp.eFlags, followed by OWORDs at 1356/1372/1388/
                   1404/1420/1436 = the two trajectories
    1696 .. 1808   centity scalars (AW puts `flags` immediately after nextState)

### PROVEN fields (named in the IDB; everything else left as explicit gaps)

    +48    float origin[3]      vec3 copy in sub_45540
    +1168  __int16 number       94 hits
    +1170  u16 otherEntityNum   17 hits
    +1178  u8 eType             108 hits
    +1201  char clientNum       18 hits. **1-BASED** -- the engine does `-1`
    +1316  int weapon           CG_GetWeaponName passes cent+1316
    +1340  int lerp_eFlags      28 hits
    +1696  u8 flags             bit0 = in use. **197 hits, the most-used field**

`struct centity_s` is defined in the S2 IDB at exactly **1808 bytes**, and
`CG_GetEntity` (0x13A00) is typed `centity_s *(int localClientNum, unsigned
entnum)`. All 306 callers now decompile with real field names:

    v13 = CG_GetEntity(v1, (unsigned __int16)v11);
    if ( (v13->flags & 1) != 0 )
    eType = v13->eType;
    v23 = 4704LL * v13->clientNum + CG_GetLocalClientGlobals(v1) + 3878296;

⚠ After changing a callee prototype you MUST `ida_hexrays.mark_cfunc_dirty(ea)`
on the callers -- IDA caches inferred local types per function and will keep
showing raw offsets otherwise. That one call is the difference between the struct
appearing to do nothing and it working.

### The gaps are load-bearing

Unmapped regions are explicit `_unk_XXX` arrays, so an unmapped field SHOWS. It
immediately exposed one: `*(_QWORD *)&Entity->_unk_49B[5]` = **+1184**, used as a
48-bit mask (`>> 13 & (1 << n) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF`). AW's entityState_s has
`partBits[8]` / `clientMask` / `threatMask` in that role. Not yet named -- the
exact one is unproven.

### ⛔ CORRECTED — the "+48 origin produced inf" mystery

CLAUDE.md recorded `ENTITY_ORIGIN = 48` as suspect because using it yielded `inf`
and 3.9e17, and player_box.cpp was left flagged as unreliable on that basis.
**The offset was right all along.** sub_45540 does `sub_AF9B70(cent + 48, out)` --
a vec3 copy. What was wrong was the POINTER: CG_GetEntity inspects its own return
address (Arxan), so calling it from the mod does not return what a game-side
caller gets (RULE A22). Origin at +48 stands.

## Naming CG_GetEntity

`sub_13A00` -> **CG_GetEntity**, behaviour-proven DESCRIPTIVE (not ported): ~15
return sites all computing `qword_8B0DB18 + 1808 * ((localClientNum << 11) +
entnum)`, 306 callers overwhelmingly CG_*. AW has no exact twin -- its
CG_GetEntityState returns `entityState_s*`, a different thing.

# ⭐⭐⭐⭐ clc / clientConnection_t MAPPED — AND 0x20140 IS FINALLY EXPLAINED
# (2026-08-17). Full struct: re/clientConnection.h

The doctrine at the top of this file opens with a state-ownership failure it
never resolved:

    "Our previous implementation wrote a recorded sequence into clc + 0x20140.
     IDA subsequently demonstrated that 0x20140 was not the field we had assumed
     it was."   ... and, much later: "Still unproven: 0x20140."

**It is now proven, and the reason it resisted identification for months is that
it CANNOT be identified by analogy: S2 inserts a dword at +131392 that has no
counterpart in the reference build (or in Q3).**

## THE METHOD — disassembly displacements, not decompiler output

`re/map_global_struct.py` regexes pseudocode and got **11** offsets out of clc's
122 referencing functions, because IDA renders the dominant access form as

    v18 = (char *)clc + 482656 * v14 + 262480;
    *(_DWORD *)((char *)clc + v17 + 262752) = 2;

— the per-client stride hides in one variable and the base constant folds into
another. Chasing that means chasing every rendering IDA might choose.

`re/map_global_disasm.py` (new) taints the register receiving the global and
records the displacement of any memory operand based on it. Machine code has no
such freedom: `mov [rax+rcx+40260h], edx` states the displacement outright.

    decompiler regex :  11 offsets
    disassembly      :  80 offsets, from 122 functions

**GENERALISE: when a struct is reached through a GLOBAL rather than an accessor,
go to the disassembly. The decompiler's freedom to re-render is the enemy.**

## ⭐⭐ THE SIZE IS A PROOF, NOT AN ASSUMPTION

Built purely from field offsets, the struct comes to **exactly 482,656 bytes** —
the per-client array stride, derived independently from the `482656 * client`
term. Two unrelated routes, same number. A layout wrong anywhere in the middle
would not land on it.

Two more fell out of the demo block, neither designed for:

    262788 + 79356 == 342144   (the next observed field)
      -> clc+262760 IS the .demo file header and is EXACTLY 79,384 bytes, the
         value the header's own +0x04 field carries and CL_Demo_Play_f validates.
         The struct reproduces the file format.
    342144 + 3984  == 346128   (again the next observed field)
      -> the footer body is exactly the 3984 tag CL_Demo_ReadFooter requires.

And 17 of 17 offsets this file had proved by hand over months were recovered
independently, including all four heavy ones: +312 (25 hits), +131396 (18),
+262744 (18), +346144 (28).

## ⭐⭐⭐ THE S2-ONLY FIELD

The AW->S2 shift is MONOTONIC (differences come from insertions, never removals),
so a +8 shift below and +12 above forces exactly one 4-byte insertion between:

    S2 offset   AW offset   shift   field
    ----------------------------------------------------------
     131388      131380      +8     serverMessageSequence
     131392        --         --    <-- S2-ONLY.  0x20140.
     131396      131384      +12    serverCommandSequence
     131400      131388      +12    lastExecutedServerCommand
     131404      131392      +12    serverCommands[128][1024]

Writing a sequence number into 0x20140 was not "the wrong sequence field" — it
was a field with no sequence semantics at all, in a game that had ADDED it. The
extractor sees it 16 times from CL_Disconnect, CL_InitCGame and CL_ParseSnapshot,
so it is real and load-bearing. **Its MEANING is still UNKNOWN. Do not write it.**

## ⛔ CORRECTED — two notes in this file contradicted each other

    the doctrine says   incoming message sequence -> 0x2013C (131388)
                        server reliable sequence  -> 0x138   (312)
    the demo note says  snapshot sequence -> 0x2013C, message sequence -> 0x138

Both cannot hold. Settled from the disassembly, and **THE DOCTRINE IS RIGHT.**
With the struct applied, CL_Demo_ProcessPacket_Type2_3 decompiles to:

    v5->lastPacketTime = cls_realtime;
    Long = MSG_ReadLong(&v10);
    v5->reliableAcknowledge = Long & 0x7FFFFFFF;
    reliableSequence = v5->reliableSequence;
    if ( v5->reliableAcknowledge >= reliableSequence - 128 )
        ... CL_ParseServerMessage ...
    else
        v5->reliableAcknowledge = reliableSequence;

That is Q3's server-message preamble VERBATIM, and this file's own decode of that
gate already used the literal 128 — which IS MAX_RELIABLE_COMMANDS. So +312 is
reliableAcknowledge, +308 is reliableSequence (both "reliable sequences", as the
doctrine said), and +131388 is serverMessageSequence. The demo note had the pair
swapped.

`lastPacketTime = cls_realtime` also turned a shift-0 inference at +8 into a
behaviour proof, for free, after the fact.

## ⛔ AND demo_game.hpp:460-463 IS WRONG

It records "CLC_RELIABLE_ACKNOWLEDGE (0x20144) and CLC_SERVER_COMMAND_SEQUENCE
are the same field". They are two DIFFERENT fields 131,084 bytes apart:
reliableAcknowledge is at +312 (0x138); 0x20144 is serverCommandSequence.

The CG_ExecuteNewServerCommands clamp built on that reading is still HARMLESS —
it clamps serverCommandSequence to itself, so it remains a no-op exactly as this
file already concluded. But the stated REASON for it is untrue. Do not extend
that reasoning, and do not "fix" the clamp.

## What is NOT mapped

Everything past +346160 is one 136,496-byte gap. AW puts netchan,
netchanOutgoingBuffer, netchanIncomingBuffer, OOBProf and the stat-packet fields
there, and S2 clearly has equivalents (the extractor sees +346160..+346192, plus
+425048..+425056 from CL_Demo_FreeCameraMove and +482376/+482384 from
CL_Disconnect / CL_WritePacket) — but the shift is unknown that deep and none of
it is proven from S2's own code. **Do not extrapolate.**

Likewise the 8-byte insertion in the head sits somewhere in 44..296, the region
AW fills with serverAddress / connect state / serverMessage[256]. The extractor
sees NO accesses at all in 44..304, which is what an error-string buffer touched
only by string functions looks like — nothing contradicts it, but the split is
unknown, so that whole region is one explicit gap.

## STATE

    re/clientConnection.h    the struct + the full derivation
    re/map_global_disasm.py  the extractor
    re/s2_clc_offsets.json   the 80 raw offsets

`clc` @ 0x1BD3D00 is typed `clientConnection_t*` in the IDB, 122 cfuncs marked
dirty so the fields show up in every decompile. IDB saved.

All four RE struct headers (centity_s, playerState_s, clientDemoPlayback,
clientConnection) COMPILE CLEAN under MSVC /std:c++17 — every static_assert
holds, including `sizeof(clientConnection_t) == 482656`. That compile is now the
regression test for the struct work; re-run it after any edit:

    cl /nologo /std:c++17 /Zs /EHsc /I. <a TU that includes all four>

Naming audit: PASS, no hard findings.

# ⭐⭐⭐ THE CUSTOM THEATER — clc BASE FIXED, AND THREE OF THIS FILE'S OWN
# THEATER NOTES WERE STALE (2026-08-17)

USER DECISION: keep and fully fix the CUSTOM (.dm_s2) demo system rather than
retire it in favour of native. That reverses the standing "retire the theater"
plan recorded above. It is a much better bet than it was, because the clc mapping
done the same day turns the theater's central mechanism from guesswork into
checkable code.

## ⭐ THE ONE REAL DEFECT — demo_game::clc_for() READ THE WRONG GLOBAL. FIXED.

    0x1BD2C00_b == IDA 0x1BD3C00 == off_1BD3C00    3 xrefs, none client code
                                                   (sub_303D0, sub_3D6030, and
                                                    sub_E7980 — the 2D HUD drawer)
    0x1BD2D00_b == IDA 0x1BD3D00 == clc            122 xrefs

The literal had been 0x100 too low since it was written, and the comment ON THAT
LINE already said 0x1BD3D00 — only the number was wrong. CLAUDE.md has recorded
this as a known-unfixed bug for a long time, deferred because "it is in working
custom-demo code". With clc now fully mapped the deferral no longer applies.

**Two measured consequences, both now fixed:**

  1. `demo_recording::pack_network()` read the message sequence through it, so
     EVERY .dm_s2 record stored `seq = 0`. That is why the transcoder had to
     renumber packets, and why it got the numbering wrong until it was changed to
     recover the real sequence from the payload instead.

  2. **The theater's message-sequence commit edge never reached the engine.**
     `commit_live_message_state()` and the feed in demo_utils.cpp restore
     serverMessageSequence and reliableAcknowledge around every replayed message —
     a faithful transcription of sub_99960's live behaviour — and every one of
     those WRITES landed in an unrelated object. CL_ParseServerMessage then read
     the real clc, which still held whatever it had. Worse, when that bogus
     pointer was null, `if (auto* clc = clc_for(0))` skipped the restore
     ENTIRELY, so the sequences were never established at all.

## ⛔ CORRECTION TO MY OWN RISK ASSESSMENT, MADE THE SAME HOUR

I first told the user this fix was risky because it "makes theater writes live in
code that was tuned around them being misdirected". **That was wrong.** Reading
the feed shows the writes are a transcription of the engine's own live commit
edge — they were ALWAYS meant to hit real clc. Nothing was tuned around the
misdirection; it is pure bug. Overstating the risk nearly deferred a real fix for
a second time.

**And the field choices were right all along.** The feed recovers the two leading
dwords from the message payload (`entry-8`, `entry-4`) and writes them to 0x2013C
and 312. Against re/clientConnection.h those are exactly serverMessageSequence
and reliableAcknowledge. Note it reads them from the PAYLOAD, not from the
container's seq field — so OLD .dm_s2 recordings (the ones with seq = 0) still
replay correctly. The fix changes WHERE the values go, never WHAT they are.

## Constant names corrected in demo_game.hpp (values unchanged, zero behaviour change)

    308 / 312               were SWAPPED. 308 is reliableSequence, 312 is
                            reliableAcknowledge. CL_Demo_ProcessPacket_Type2_3 is
                            Q3's preamble verbatim, and the clamp's literal 128
                            IS MAX_RELIABLE_COMMANDS.
    0x20144                 named reliableAcknowledge; it is serverCommandSequence.
                            That mislabel is what produced the untrue justification
                            for the CG_ExecuteNewServerCommands clamp. The clamp
                            itself stays a benign no-op — do NOT "fix" it.
    CLC_LAST_SNAPSHOT_...   an INVENTED name for 0x20140. Retired to
                            CLC_S2_ONLY_0x20140 with a never-write warning, since
                            0x20140 is now proven to be an S2-only field of
                            unknown meaning. demo_utils.cpp already avoided
                            touching it — that instinct was right, for a better
                            reason than it was written for.

Back-compat aliases keep every existing call site compiling unchanged.

## ⛔⛔ THREE THEATER NOTES IN THIS FILE ARE STALE — DO NOT ACT ON THEM

Found by reading the code instead of the record. Anyone resuming theater work
should re-verify before "fixing" anything else here:

  1. **"the theater's PLAYBACK half is still stuck at GATE D,
     DObj_MaterialsReady"** — STALE. The proven viewmodel fix
     (`request_viewmodel_stream` -> sub_196220, user-confirmed in game) is gated
     on `playback_active()`, which is
     `g_native_playing || demo_playback::is_active_replay()`. The theater has had
     it all along. The same is true of the remote-player world-model request
     (`bg_get_world_model_stub` uses the same gate).

  2. **"our 20 Hz theater clock is the leading explanation for playback not

  3. **"demo_game::clc_for() reads the WRONG GLOBAL ... NOT fixed"** — fixed now.

So the theater's genuinely-open defect list was ONE item, not four. The record had
drifted because fixes landed in demo_native.cpp and were written up as native
wins without noting that the shared gate covers theater too.

## LESSON — the written record decays faster than the code

Three of four "known theater problems" were already solved. I nearly spent a
build fixing the viewmodel a second time. **When resuming an area after a gap,
grep the code for the fix before trusting a note that says it is broken** — and
when a fix lands behind a SHARED gate, say in the write-up which systems it
covers, not just the one you were testing.

The clc fix is the only substantive behaviour change, and its effect (the engine

Test: record a .dm_s2 (`demo_start` / `demoautorecord 1`), play it back in the

## ⚠ BUILD-TOOL WEDGE, SECOND OCCURRENCE — AND HOW I CAUSED IT

An orphaned `cl.exe` sat holding the PDB for **4 hours** (pid alive 14,779s, no
MSBuild parent) and wedged every subsequent build with
`C1041: cannot open program database`.

I caused it by launching a second build while the first was still running. I DID
run `Get-Process cl,MSBuild` first — but in the SAME command as the build, so it
printed "cl 37800 running" and then built anyway. **A check you do not gate on is

delete the stale pdb, build once with `-m:1`.

# ⭐⭐⭐⭐ THE NATIVE DEMO APPENDER — LOCATED, AND THE MOD WAS ALREADY CALLING IT
# (2026-08-17). Found by a user observation, not by searching.

## The observation

USER, testing build 818516D4 (the clc base fix) on an EXISTING .dm_s2:

  * the viewmodel fix works in the CUSTOM theater — CONFIRMS that
    `playback_active()` covering `is_active_replay()` was always enough, and that
    this file's "theater is stuck at GATE D" note was stale;
  * **the engine started recording a NATIVE .demo during custom theater playback**,
    and that .demo then PLAYED BACK correctly.

The second was unexpected. It is fully explained, and it closes an open question.

## ⭐ CLAUDE.md HAS SAID FOR MONTHS THAT THIS FUNCTION WAS NEVER FOUND

The earlier record states plainly:

    "NOT in CL_ParseServerMessage @0x4649D0 -- decompiled in full, no demo write.
     NOT through the write callback clc+346136 ... Nothing per-snapshot.
     So ongoing packets are buffered somewhere else and flushed by
     CL_Demo_StopRecord. The appender has not been located."

**It is `sub_91CFA0` / `sub_91D2A0` / `sub_91CEC0`, and `src/demo/demo_utils.cpp`
has been calling all three since it was written** — under the name "message event
functions", which is why nobody recognised them.

## The chain, from sub_99960 (the live receive loop)

    MSG_ReadLong                       serverMessageSequence
    MSG_ReadLong                       reliableAcknowledge
    CL_ParseServerMessage
    sub_910440                         "message ready"
    CL_Demo_IsRecordPendingFirstSnapshot   0x91C6C0  <- the gate
    CL_Demo_RecordMessage_Begin            0x91CFA0
    CL_Demo_RecordMessage_Data             0x91D2A0  (state, client, seq, data, len)
    CL_Demo_RecordMessage_End              0x91CEC0

`demo_utils::commit_live_message_state()` replicates that tail EXACTLY, passing
`msg.data + 4, msg.cursize - 4` and the recovered `incoming_message_sequence`. It
was written to reproduce sub_99960's commit edge for correctness; nobody realised
half of it was the recorder.

## ⭐⭐ WHY IT ONLY STARTED WORKING NOW — IT IS THE clc FIX

    const auto record_state = *(std::uintptr_t*)(clc + 346136);
    if (!record_state || ...) return;

`clc` there comes from `clc_for()`, which until today read the WRONG GLOBAL. So
`record_state` came back 0 (or junk) and the append returned on EVERY message,
silently. Correcting the base made clc+346136 the real state pointer, and the
append began landing.

So "it did something weird" was the fix working. This is also independent
confirmation that the clc base fix is real and reaches live behaviour.

## ⛔ CORRECTED — my own struct field name, within the hour

I named clc+346132 `demoIsRecording`, from a CLAUDE.md annotation rather than from
code. That is exactly what the Absolute Rule forbids, and it was wrong:

    CL_Demo_StartRecord                      sets it to 1
    CL_Demo_NoteFirstSnapshotForRecord       0x91C6E0, SOLE CALLER CL_ParseSnapshot:
                                             if set, CLEARS it and stores its second
                                             argument into demoFooterBody+8
    the per-message append                   runs only when it reads 0

So it means **"recording armed, still waiting for a snapshot to anchor to"**, not
"recording". Renamed `demoRecordPendingFirstSnapshot`, and clc+346136 renamed
`demoRecordMessageState` (it is the append trio's arg0, not merely a write
callback). Struct still sums to 482656.

Both small predicates are BODY-PROVEN. The append trio is CALL-SITE-PROVEN only --
their bodies are Arxan dispatch thunks (`sub_AF9B70`), so the individual roles of
Begin/Data/End are inferred from the argument shapes and the observed result. The
IDB comments say so; re-check before depending on the split.

## ⭐ WHAT THIS UNLOCKS — a zero-tooling .dm_s2 -> .demo transcode

`tools/s2_dm_to_demo.py` exists to convert our container into a native one, and it
needs a same-map template for the header blob and the NetConstStrings footer.
Playing a .dm_s2 in the theater now produces a native .demo **written by the engine
itself**, so it carries:

  * the engine's own 79,384-byte header (built from live state, no template),
  * the engine's own footer + NCS table for that session,
  * the correct map name at footer+272.

That removes the transcoder's template requirement entirely for anything we can
replay. The offline tool remains useful for batch work and for demos we cannot or
do not want to replay.

⚠ NOT YET CHECKED: whether the auto type-21 footer repair (hooked on
CL_Demo_StopRecord) fires at the end of a theater playback the same way it does
after a live match. If a theater-produced .demo will not play, check its footer
type 21 first -- the GUI's "Fix Selected Demo" button repairs it.

⚠ ALSO: this now happens on EVERY theater playback, because native recording is
enabled by default and the hub gate (byte_1BD36F8) is open on a real map. That is
free transcoding, but it is also unrequested disk usage. If it becomes a nuisance
the honest fix is a toggle, not removing the commit-edge replication -- the append
chain is a faithful part of sub_99960 and dropping it would change what the theater
reproduces.

This was not found by searching for it. It was found because the user reported a

# ⭐⭐⭐ STEPPY CUSTOM-DEMO PLAYBACK — MEASURED AND FIXED (2026-08-17)

USER: theater playback "definitely steppy, ugly". Two prior explanations in this
file were already fixed and were NOT the cause. The real one was found in one
24-frame burst.

## THE MEASUREMENT — `demo_lerp`, sampled inside CG_DrawActiveFrame

CG_DrawActiveFrame runs at RENDER rate (~230/s measured) while the theater's feed
and clock tick once per CLIENT frame (20/s). That is the axis the problem lives
on, so the probe samples there rather than from Present. One bounded 24-frame
burst (RULE A18 — a per-frame probe with a finite answer must not stream).

    serverTime=291244 (d=+6) snap=291250 lead= +6  pinned=291221
    serverTime=291250 (d=+6) snap=291250 lead= +0  pinned=291221
    serverTime=291257 (d=+7) snap=291250 lead= -7  pinned=291221
    serverTime=291263 (d=+6) snap=291250 lead=-13  pinned=291221
    serverTime=291270 (d=+7) snap=291300 lead=+30  pinned=291271

## PROVEN — the clock was never the problem

`clientActive.serverTime` rose on EVERY rendered frame (d = +5..+16, never 0), so
`g_smooth_clock` does exactly what it claims. Anything that blames the theater
clock for stepping is wrong; stop looking there.

## ⭐ PROVEN — the cause is `lead` (snap - serverTime) GOING NEGATIVE

Across the 24 samples, lead ran
  +1 -13 +21 +8 +2 -4 -10 -16 +28 +23 +19 +12 +6 +0 -7 -13 +30 +18 +13 +6 -1 -9 -16 +26

**9 of 24 frames -- 38% -- had lead <= 0.** A negative lead means the time being
rendered has run PAST the newest parsed snapshot, so there is no forward snapshot
to interpolate toward and those frames snap to the last known state. High FPS,
smooth clock, stepped motion.

## The gate was wrong in TWO ways at once

    old:  return demo_game::snap_server_time() <= demo_game::server_time();

  1. **WRONG CLOCK.** `server_time()` is the GLOBAL cl_serverTime, which
     `set_theater_server_time()` pins once per CLIENT frame. The renderer
     interpolates at `clientActive.serverTime` instead, which advances per RENDER
     frame. In the burst, `pinned` trails `serverTime` by up to 42 ms -- so the
     feed decided when to pull the next snapshot using a clock that lags the one
     doing the drawing.

  2. **NO LEAD.** Even against the right clock, feeding "until the snapshot passes
     now" leaves lead ~= 0, and it goes negative the moment the render clock
     advances. Live play never looks like this: the client deliberately holds
     render time BEHIND the newest snapshot by about one snapshot interval, and
     that gap is what the interpolator aims across. S2's cadence is 20 Hz
     (CL_ClientFrame does cl_serverTime += 50), so one interval is 50 ms.

## THE FIX

    int g_interp_lead_ms = 50;              // one snapshot interval

    bool continue_demo_reading()
    {
        int now = demo_game::server_time();
        if (void* cl = demo_game::client_active_for(0))
        {
            const int st = demo_game::read_i(cl, demo_game::CA_SERVER_TIME);
            if (st > 0) now = st;
        }
        return demo_game::snap_server_time() <= now + g_interp_lead_ms;
    }

Feeding further ahead does NOT play the demo faster -- it only makes the data
available earlier. The clock is untouched, so seek, pause and timescale are
unaffected. Predicted lead after the fix: roughly +34..+80, i.e. always positive.

    demo_lead        report the current lead
    demo_lead 0      restore the OLD gate -- reproduces the stepping on demand
    demo_lerp        re-run the 24-frame burst to confirm lead stays positive

Both are kept deliberately: the A/B is the verification, and `demo_lead 0` means a
future session can reproduce the defect instead of taking this write-up on trust.

## ⛔ THREE HYPOTHESES KILLED ON THE WAY -- do not re-run them

  1. **"stale clc sequence state makes CL_ParseSnapshot drop delta snapshots."**
     Dead: the consumers of the two fields the theater restores are
     CL_ParseServerMessage / the demo recorders (serverMessageSequence) and
     CL_WritePacket / CL_Disconnect (reliableAcknowledge). NEITHER is read by
     CL_ParseSnapshot or by any interpolation code. **The clc base fix is not a
     smoothness fix** -- it is real, but its reach is the recorder append and the
     container's seq field.
  2. **"the feed never leaves a forward snapshot."** Half right, and the wrong
     half: the gate's SHAPE (feed while snap <= clock) does leave one ahead. What
     it lacked was the right clock and any margin.
  3. **"we smoothed the wrong clock -- the renderer follows the pinned global."**
     Dead: serverTime advanced every rendered frame, so the renderer follows the
     smooth one. The pinned global's fault was feeding the GATE, not the drawing.

## Does this apply to existing demos?

YES, and so does the clc fix. The feed recovers each message's sequences from the
message PAYLOAD (entry-8 / entry-4), not from the container's seq field, so old
.dm_s2 files are unaffected by the recorder-side change. Nothing about either fix
is new-recordings-only.

## METHOD NOTE

Three wrong hypotheses in a row, each killed cheaply by asking "who actually READS
this field" before building anything. The one build that was spent went on a
MEASUREMENT, not a guess, and the measurement named the cause in a single burst.
Reading consumer lists is much cheaper than reading control flow.

# ✅ SMOOTH CUSTOM-DEMO PLAYBACK — FIXED AND CONFIRMED IN GAME (2026-08-17)

USER CONFIRMED: "everything is so smooth now". All five Fix Declaration conditions
met. Two defects, found in that order, each measured before it was touched.

## DEFECT 1 (at 1x) — the feed gate used the wrong clock

Measured with `demo_lerp`, a bounded 24-frame burst sampled inside
CG_DrawActiveFrame (render rate) rather than from Present:

    serverTime=291250 (d=+6) snap=291250 lead= +0  pinned=291221
    serverTime=291257 (d=+7) snap=291250 lead= -7  pinned=291221
    serverTime=291263 (d=+6) snap=291250 lead=-13  pinned=291221
    serverTime=291270 (d=+7) snap=291300 lead=+30  pinned=291271

`lead` (snap - serverTime) was <= 0 on 9 of 24 frames -- 38%. Those frames render
past the newest snapshot, so there is no forward target and they hold the last
state. THAT is the stepping.

Cause: `continue_demo_reading()` gated on `demo_game::server_time()` -- the GLOBAL
cl_serverTime, pinned once per CL_ClientFrame -- while the renderer interpolates at
clientActive.serverTime. `pinned` trailed by up to 42 ms, so the gate said "snap is
still ahead, do not feed" while the renderer had already passed it, and the feed sat
idle for 3-4 frames.

FIX: gate on clientActive.serverTime, which is native's own shape
(`serverTime >= snap.serverTime` in CL_SetCGameTime's feed loop), plus an optional
lead margin. `demo_lead 0` restores the no-margin native form; `demo_lead` reports it.

## DEFECT 2 (off 1x) — the pinned clock value only changed 20 times a second

USER: "it was smooth until the moment I messed with timescale".

Off 1x, `smooth_clock_active()` is false and the theater re-stamps serverTime
directly after CL_SetCGameTime_orig. That re-stamp ALREADY ran at render rate --
CL_SetCGameTime runs per rendered frame, which the burst above proves (serverTime
moved every frame). **But the value it stamped, `demo_clock_ms()`, only changed 20
times a second, because `advance_clock()` was called solely from CL_ClientFrame.**
Pinning serverTime to a 20 Hz value IS the staircase.

FIX: call `g_play.advance_clock()` immediately before the re-stamp, so the stamped
value changes every rendered frame. One line, in the place the value is consumed.

## ⛔ AND A WRONG FIX I SHIPPED AND REVERTED THE SAME HOUR

I first made `smooth_clock_active()` return `g_smooth_clock` unconditionally,
believing the PIN was the problem, and moved the clock write into
CG_DrawActiveFrame as a delta-only update. That was wrong twice over:

  * the pin was never the problem -- it already ran at render rate; the VALUE was
    stale;
  * removing it would BREAK SLOW MOTION, because CL_SetCGameTime ratchets:
        serverTime = serverTimeDelta + cls_realtime;
        if (serverTime < oldFrameServerTime) serverTime = oldFrameServerTime;
    Below 1x a delta-derived clock overshoots the scaled target and the ratchet
    makes that unrecoverable. That is exactly why the 1x restriction exists.

The 1x restriction is now documented in the code as load-bearing so it does not get
"simplified" again.

## AUDIT — the custom theater against the native path

Asked for before testing: does the theater behave the way a native demo would.

MATCHES NATIVE
  * the feed is driven from CL_SetCGameTime -- the same function native's feed loop
    lives in, at the same rate. (It is called from `cl_set_cgame_time_stub`.)
  * the feed condition now gates on serverTime, native's shape.
  * `newSnapshots` suppression at non-1x is CORRECT. I flagged it as a divergence,
    then the S2 decompile settled it: the tail is
        if (newSnapshots) CL_AdjustTimeDelta();
    so that field gates ONLY AdjustTimeDelta, not snapshot transitions. Zeroing it
    is a targeted, correct way to stop the engine fighting the theater clock.
  * rewind clears the ratchet: demo_game.hpp writes CA_OLD_SERVER_TIME and
    CA_OLD_FRAME_SERVER_TIME on restart, so a backward seek is not blocked by it.

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCES, all sound
  * pause: native freezes cls_realtime onto the demo clock
    (cls_realtime = serverTime - 5 - serverTimeDelta); the theater instead corrects
    serverTimeDelta so serverTime lands on the snapshot. Equivalent.
  * seek: native uses the 250-slot keyframe ring; the theater restarts the stream.
  * timescale: theater uses its own dvar, native uses PlaybackData+28. Separate
    systems by design.

ADDED BEYOND NATIVE
  * the feed lead margin (default 50 ms = one snapshot interval). Native has none.
    With the gate on the right clock and the feed running after
    CL_SetCGameTime_orig, lead should already be positive at draw time without it,
    so `demo_lead 0` is the native-faithful setting and is worth testing -- if 1x
    is smooth at 0, drop the margin rather than keep a compensation.

## ⭐ NATIVE RECORDING DURING THEATER PLAYBACK IS NOW OPT-IN

Replaying a .dm_s2 also wrote a native .demo, because
`commit_live_message_state()` replicates sub_99960's commit edge and part of that
edge IS the recorder's append chain. Useful -- it is a free .dm_s2 -> .demo
transcode with the engine's own header, footer and NCS table, no same-map template
-- but nobody asked for it and it silently writes a multi-megabyte file on every
playback.

Blocked at the GATE (CL_Demo_IsRecordingAllowed), not at the append. Suppressing
only the append would still open the file and write a header and footer, leaving a
packet-less .demo that looks valid and is not.

    demo_record_theater        toggle    (default OFF)
    demo_record_theater 1      opt in -- arm BEFORE demo_play, since
                               CL_Demo_StartRecord only runs at cgame init

Ordering is safe: `start_file()` opens the demo before `bootstrap_map()`, so
`demo_playback::is_playing()` is already true when CL_InitCGame reaches
CL_Demo_StartRecord.

## ⚠ BUILD NOTE — DO NOT GATE A BUILD ON MSBuild.exe

MSBuild leaves ~12 idle NODE-REUSE workers alive for 15 minutes after a build.
They are not an active compile, so a "wait until MSBuild is gone" loop blocks for a
quarter of an hour. Gate on `cl.exe` / `link.exe` only -- those exist solely while
compiling -- and pass `/nodeReuse:false` to avoid leaving the workers at all.
(Separately: a genuinely ORPHANED cl.exe holding the PDB is the other failure mode,
and that one does need killing.)

## Method 1 — string anchors (re/mwrpc_harvest.py, mwrpc_score.py)

`re/mwr_anchors.json` (35,882 PS4 anchors -> named PS4 function) already existed
from the S2 work. Only **3,725 (10.4%) are present in MWR-PC** — expected, and
the same effect CLAUDE.md already records for S2: MWR-PS4 is a DEBUG build whose
anchors are mostly assert text (source paths, condition expressions), and the PC
build is RELEASE with asserts stripped. 3,195 of those carry a PC code xref.

Filters, all from the skill: anchor unambiguous on BOTH sides, unanimous vote,
one-name-one-function, never overwrite, distinctiveness (not length).

## ⭐ Method 2 — same-game call-graph propagation (re/mwrpc_propagate.py)

With a partial mapping M: pc_ea -> ps4_ea, an unmapped PC function X is
constrained by every mapped neighbour:

    from callees : candidates = INTERSECT over mapped callee c of callers_ps4(M[c])
    from callers : candidates = INTERSECT over mapped caller p of callees_ps4(M[p])

Require >= 2 independent supporting neighbours and exactly ONE surviving
candidate. Uses NO string evidence, so it is a genuine second source. Iterated to
a fixed point — each name resolved tightens its neighbours, so rounds compound
WITHOUT loosening the rule.

## ⭐⭐ MEASURED PRECISION — hide known-good pairs and re-derive them

`re/mwrpc_holdout.py`. Hide 20% of the anchor-verified pairs, propagate from the
rest, check whether propagation rediscovers them. 5 trials:

    min_sup  size_gate  recovered  correct  wrong  precision  recall
       2       none        125       123      2     98.40%    17.2%
       2       <=3.0        86        83      3     96.51%    11.9%
       3       none         50        49      1     98.00%     6.9%
       3       <=3.0        33        33      0    100.00%     4.6%

## ⛔ CORRECTED — FUNCTION SIZE IS NOT A VALIDITY SIGNAL HERE

I distrusted matches with wild size ratios (`CG_EntityEvent` PC 1063 vs PS4
23472 bytes) and added a size gate. **The holdout says the gate makes precision
WORSE (96.5% vs 98.4%) and costs a third of the recall.** Debug-vs-release plus
different compilers (MSVC vs Clang) make size divergence normal between these two
builds. Do not gate on size, and do not re-add it "for safety".

Note this is the OPPOSITE of the S2 Steam<->Xbox case, where same-compiler builds
matched 99.9% by size. The distinction is same-toolchain, not same-game.

## ⛔ CORRECTED — MY FIRST HOLDOUT WAS CONTAMINATED

I first validated against the 225 pre-existing PC names and measured a worrying
71%. That number is void: those names are earlier analyst work of unknown rigor,
and this file's own doctrine says not to treat them as ground truth. Both
"failures" were very likely the PRE-EXISTING name being wrong:

  * 0x29d8a0 existing `G_InitializeAmmo`, anchors `m_maxWidth` + `m_maxScore`
    (two LUI scorebar property names) -> LUIElement_UIScorebarLayout
  * 0x561b50 existing `SV_EndClientMessage` vs PS4 `SV_EndClientSnapshot` from
    `EXE_SERVERMESSAGEOVERFLOW` — adjacent functions; the PS4 side is a REAL
    symbol, the PC name was a guess

Both left alone (Contradiction Rule: drop, do not pick a winner). **Validate
against an independent EVIDENCE SOURCE, not against unverified prior names.**

## ⭐⭐ Method 3 — binding tables, and the off-by-one that nearly poisoned them

MWR-PC has large self-naming `{const char* name, void* fn}` tables (338, 149,
134, 117, 107 entries...). Tier-1 evidence — but the first scanner aliased
badly: it reported the same table at stride 16/32/48/64, and the two stride-16
readings DISAGREED, one pairing 0xba1b0 with `OpenOldMenu` and the other with
`PlaySound`. A shifted reading silently mis-names an entire table.

Two fixes:
  * find MAXIMAL runs of alternating [str ptr][fn ptr] so a base can never start
    mid-record (re/mwrpc_tables2.py);
  * settle the alignment EMPIRICALLY rather than by assumption — check both
    readings against names already derived from strings and call graph:
        reading A (name+0, fn+8):  58% agreement
        reading B (name+8, fn+0):   0% agreement
    A is the canonical luaL_Reg shape, and the data agrees.

Then, per the skill, **match TABLES to TABLES before matching entries** — a bare
binding name (`IsEnabled`, `GetTime`, `show`) means different things in different
tables. 31 table pairs matched at ratio 0.96-1.0; entries matched only inside a
corresponding pair. This yields PS4's REAL symbols (`LUI_CoD_LuaCall_*`) rather
than synthesized `Lua_<Lib>_<Binding>` names.

**Validated 43/43 (100%)** against names derived independently from anchors and
propagation.

    named in .text        573 (6.38%)  ->  1,239 (13.79%)
    named, >= 256 bytes    91 (3.48%)  ->    451 (17.25%)   <- 5x on the ones
                                                               that matter
    audit: PASS, 0 hard findings (0 duplicate, 0 phantom reference)

Reference = port 18337. Target = port 19337. Both registered in re/ida.py as
`cod4` / `cod4x`. No session restart was needed: the MCP namespaces only exist
if the server was up at session start, and direct JSON-RPC via re/ida.py is the
documented fallback (it works identically).

## ⭐⭐⭐ PORT 18337 IS THE **macOS** BUILD, NOT A WINDOWS CoD4

This is the single fact the whole pass turns on, and it is not what the name
"named cod4 idb" suggests:

    idb  E:\Leaked PDBS and IDBS\COD4\Call of Duty 4 Multiplayer.i64
    Mach-O: segments __text / __cstring / __const / __bss / __common,
            Objective-C sections, ASIHTTPRequest + Cocoa classes,
            ODE physics (dMessage, dJointCreateAMotor), OpenGL, AudioUnit
    imagebase 0x1000        (CoD4X is a PE at 0x400000)
    9,140 functions, 100% named

So it is the Aspyr macOS port with a full symbol table. Consequences:

  * **7,364 of 9,140 symbols are Itanium C++-mangled** and they are the ACTUAL
    ENGINE FUNCTIONS. 1,163 are `_`-prefixed C symbols (libc / GL / ODE / a few
    real engine ones like `_FS_FileSeek`), 527 Objective-C, 83 dunder.
  * this is a CROSS-COMPILER, CROSS-PLATFORM pair (GCC/Mach-O vs MSVC/PE), so
    **function SIZE is not evidence** and is never used as a filter. That is the
    same conclusion the MWR pass measured (a size gate made precision WORSE);
    it is NOT the S2 Steam<->Xbox case, where same-toolchain builds matched
    99.9% by size. The distinction is same-TOOLCHAIN, not same-game.

⛔ MY FIRST SCORING RUN PRODUCED **4** USABLE ANCHORS out of 2,924 available,
because the name filter rejected anything starting `__` — i.e. it threw away
every mangled symbol, which is to say the entire game. The "3,706 reference names
rejected" line in the diagnostic is what exposed it. Generalise: when a filter
rejects the overwhelming majority of a reference set, print what it is rejecting
before believing the result.

## re/demangle_itanium.py — and it is VALIDATED, not trusted

Minimal Itanium demangler recovering the qualified NAME only (arguments are
deliberately ignored; we want a name, not a prototype):

    __Z16BG_ClipForWeaponi                       -> BG_ClipForWeapon
    __ZN12CStreamSound22set_sample_ms_positionEi -> CStreamSound::set_sample_ms_position
    __ZL18DynEnt_AllocXModeli                    -> DynEnt_AllocXModel   (L = static)

Cross-checked against **IDA's own demangler** on all 7,931 symbols it could
demangle (re/check_demangle.py): **98.16% agreement**, and EVERY ONE of the 134
disagreements is a C++ TEMPLATE (`std::vector<...>`, `CCallback<...>`) where my
parser stops at the template argument list. Those are macOS-only STL
instantiations that own no shared distinctive strings, so they are rejected
outright rather than half-decoded. The demangler is therefore correct on every
symbol the pass actually uses.

`::` is written `__` in applied names, which is the convention already used in
this project for AW-vs-MWR notation.

## THE TWO METHODS, AND WHAT EACH YIELDED

    string anchors (cross-binary)                 449
    call-graph propagation (no strings)            212
    reseeding propagation loop (compounds)          10
    individually verified (see below)                4
    -----------------------------------------------------
                                                   666  net +666 named

**Anchors.** A string literal owned by exactly ONE function on BOTH sides, with
the reference name surviving cleaning. 5,087 reference strings have an owner;
4,402 also exist in CoD4X; 2,924 are usable anchors over 595 target functions.
Both binaries even share the same quirky sentence *"Cause a Com_Error if a sound
file is missing."*, which is what the up-front sanity probe (re/strprobe.py)
established before any effort went in.

**Propagation.** For an unmapped target X, intersect over every mapped
neighbour: callees give `INTERSECT callers_ref(M[c])`, callers give
`INTERSECT callees_ref(M[p])`. Require >= 2 independent supporting neighbours
and exactly ONE survivor. Uses NO strings, so it is a genuinely second source.
Iterated to a fixed point (6 rounds; +118, +64, +19, +10, +1).

## ⭐⭐ MEASURED PRECISION — k-fold, every pair checked, 4 independent shuffles

re/cod4x_crossval.py hides every anchor pair exactly once per repeat and asks
whether propagation independently rediscovers it:

    MIN_SUPPORT=2   458 answers   447 correct   11 wrong   97.60%
    MIN_SUPPORT=3   292 answers   291 correct    1 wrong   99.66%

Contradiction detection is **SEED-DEPENDENT** — whether propagation can answer
for a hidden pair depends on which of its neighbours are also hidden. A single
5-fold run found 4 contradictions; a random 20% holdout found a 5th that the
fold split never reached. So the shuffles are repeated and the contradictions
UNIONed: **8 excluded**, per the Contradiction Rule (dropped, not adjudicated):

    0x515f70 Scr_BeginLoadScripts vs FS_ListFilteredFiles
    0x530e10 SV_MasterShutdown    vs Com_Quit_f
    0x548dc0 CL_SelectStringTableEntryInDvar_f vs CL_WWWDownload
    0x4cad20 GScr_LoadGameTypeScript vs GScr_LoadScriptAndLabel
    0x52cd10 SV_ClientThink       vs MSG_ReadDeltaUsercmdKey
    0x4ef7a0 CM_LoadMapFromBsp    vs FS_ListFilteredFiles
    0x543ef6 UI_OwnerDraw         vs ReplaceDirective
    0x490770 DynEnt_LoadEntities  vs CM_LoadStaticModels

⭐ THE EXCLUSION PAID OFF VISIBLY: with 0x543ef6 dropped, the reseeding loop
then placed `UI_OwnerDraw` at **0x5438a0** on graph evidence. Dropping the
contradiction did not lose the name — it let the correct home emerge.

## ⛔ NEGATIVE RESULT — MY ANCHOR TIERING DOES NOT PREDICT CORRECTNESS

Precision measured per tier:

    multi          97.79%      dominant       100.00%
    single_strong  95.71%      single_weak     97.92%

**`single_weak` is not worse than `multi`.** So the "distinctiveness score"
tiering — carried over from the S2/AW CROSS-TITLE work, where a shared generic
string can be coincidence — does not transfer to a SAME-GAME pair, where a
uniquely-owned shared string is near-conclusive on its own and one anchor is as
good as five. All four tiers were applied. Anywhere in this file that calls
single_weak "the risky tier", that is a cross-title property, not a general one.

## COLLISIONS HAVE TWO SHAPES, AND ONLY ONE IS RECOVERABLE

60 names were claimed by 2+ target functions (153 functions).

  * **genuinely ambiguous** — `ClientCommand` proposed for five CONSECUTIVE
    functions 0x4b2bb0..0x4b2e40 spaced ~0xA0. The Mac build inlined what CoD4X
    splits into sibling handlers, so no single target deserves the name. 47 left
    dropped.
  * **overwhelmingly one-sided** — `AimAssist_Init` 72 anchors vs a neighbour
    with 1; `UI_RunMenuScript` 58 vs 4; `BG_AnimParseAnimScript` 17 vs 1. CoD4X
    split off a small helper that happens to reference one of the same strings.
    Recovered only at **>= 3x the runner-up and >= 3 anchors**: 13 names, and
    that tier measured 100%.

## ⭐⭐ Cmd_AddCommand DOES NOT EXIST AS A FUNCTION IN CoD4X — IT IS INLINED

Chased because a command table would be tier-1 self-naming evidence. Three
attempts, and the finding is the useful part:

`SV_AddOperatorCommands` (0x528870) shows the registration OPEN-CODED per
command — `off_D932298 = aHeartbeat; off_D9322A4 = nullsub_1; ...` — then calls
the server-side registrar separately. So the client-side `Cmd_AddCommand` was
inlined by the compiler and propagation could never map it, correctly.

⛔ AND THE "TIE" THAT LOOKED LIKE THE REGISTRAR WAS TWO UBIQUITOUS UTILITIES.
Caller-intersection gave 0x4f9950 and 0x4fcbc0 at 15 votes each. Inspecting
their call-site arguments (re/cod4x_callsites.py) showed 0x4fcbc0 is a PRINT
function (`(0x11, fmt, "Mantle Failed: ...")`) and 0x56c350 — the top candidate
for `Dvar_RegisterBool` at 28/30 — is the shared `Dvar_Register` internal, since
964 of its 1,028 call sites pass a dvar DESCRIPTION and it is reached from many
different `Dvar_Register*` callers. **A shared callee cannot be named after one
of its callers**, so it is commented, not named. Two near-misses avoided by
looking at arguments rather than vote counts.

## ⭐ NAMED INDIVIDUALLY (each carries its own basis, not the pass-level figure)

    0x4f9140  Cmd_AddServerCommandInternal   TIER-1 SELF-NAMING: its own error
              string is "Cmd_AddServerCommand: %s already defined\n". Signature
              from its body: (const char *name@<edi>, int fn, cmd_function_s *slot),
              writing slot[1]=name, slot[4]=fn, slot[0]=old head (dword_14099DC).
              The name arrives in EDI, which is why a push-only argument scan
              found no strings at its call sites.
    0x4fcbc0  Com_Printf                     97 of 115 mapped callers of the
              reference Com_Printf call it (runner-up 32), AND the observed
              call-site shape is (int channel, const char *fmt, ...). Independent
              corroboration: Com_DPrintf was placed at 0x4fcc10 by the anchor
              pass and scores 30/32 for the reference Com_DPrintf.
    0x462f00  goprone_f
    0x462df0  speed_throw_minus_f            both from the LIVE command list

DELIBERATELY NOT NAMED, with the reason written into the IDB: 0x56c350 (shared
Dvar_Register internal) and 0x4f9950 (the command-exists predicate used by the
inlined Cmd_AddCommand — role clear, name unproven).

## ⭐ THE DUMP'S .data IS PARTIALLY POPULATED — USEFUL, AND LIMITED

`iw3mp_dump.exe` is a dump of a RUNNING process, so the command linked-lists in
.data are live and walkable: `cmd_function_s {next@0, name@4, fn@16}` from the
registrar's own body. That recovered `goprone` -> 0x462f00 and `-speed_throw` ->
0x462df0 — genuine tier-1 pairings from the running game itself.

But both list walks terminated on `0xffffffff` after 2-4 entries: **most of the
dump's .data pages were not captured**. So the command-table route yields ~2
names here, not ~200. Recorded as a dead end WITH the reason, so nobody spends
another hour on it. (The same partial-capture caveat applies to any future
attempt to read live engine state out of this dump.)

## ⚠ AN AUDIT FIX THAT MATTERS BEYOND THIS PASS

`re/audit_names.py` first reported **2 HARD findings** against CoD4X — both false
positives, both instructive:

  * its check B compares by **S2 ADDRESS**. CoD4X's 0x58fc00 is a completely
    different function from S2's 0x58fc00, so the S2 claim files "contradicted" a
    CoD4X name that has nothing to do with them.
  * the HARD (rather than review) verdict came from **my own comment text**: the
    phrase "CoD4-Mac string-anchor port" substring-matched S2's `anchor:` source
    marker, so the audit thought the name disagreed with its OWN stated basis.
    That is exactly the "do not substring-match reference labels" trap the file
    already documents, re-triggered from a different direction.

FIXED: `--evidence s2|none` scopes address-keyed evidence to the IDB it came
from, and `--dump` stops a non-S2 audit clobbering `s2_named_dump.json`. Check D
(phantom reference) was EXTENDED to know CoD4-Mac, comparing against the
demangled/cleaned reference names — without that, every ported name looks like a
phantom. It now passes with **0 phantoms**, which is a real result: every applied
name genuinely exists in the reference.

Run it as:

    python re/audit_names.py --port 19337 --evidence none \
        --dump <abs>/re/cod4x_named_dump.json --report <abs>/re/cod4x_audit_report.json

⚠ the `--dump` path must be ABSOLUTE: IDA writes it from its own working
directory, so a relative path fails with FileNotFoundError inside the plugin.

Remaining, both benign and pre-existing: 573 "no recorded basis" are the
IDA-derived CRT/import names (`__input_l`, `__pow_pentium4`, `start_10`), and the
one "differs only by case" is three legitimately distinct MSVC `std::exception`
constructor overloads.

  3. **The 786 rejected reference names** — Objective-C, STL templates and the
     macOS-only API blocklist in `cod4x_common.MAC_ONLY`. Some legitimate shared
     third-party code is being blocked with them (libjpeg `jpeg_*`, ODE `d*`,
     zlib), and CoD4X links the same libraries. Loosening the blocklist for
     provably-shared libraries is a bounded win.
  4. **CoD4X's own additions** cannot come from the reference at all — CoD4X adds
     functions the 2007 game never had (its `goprone` is already visible). Those
     need target-only evidence.
  5. `0x56c350` — establish which `Dvar_Register` variant it is, from its type
     argument (imm 0x1/0x3/0x5 at the call sites looked like a dvar type enum).

# CoD4X PASS 2 — THE CG_ BUG, AND FOUR NEW METHODS (2026-08-17, same session)

    named   1,239 -> 1,487   (13.79% -> 16.55%)
    >=256B    451 ->   570   (17.25% -> 21.81%)
    audit PASS, 0 hard findings.  IDB saved (.i64 mtime verified).

USER SPOTTED IT: "no CG_ functions mapped at all?" - correct, and it was a bug in
my own filter, not a property of the binaries.

## ⛔⛔ THE SAME MISTAKE, TWICE, AND THE SECOND TIME AFTER I HAD WRITTEN IT DOWN

**First**: `MAC_ONLY` contained `"CG"` for Core**G**raphics, and
`n.startswith("CG")` also matches `CG_`. So the loose prefix silently deleted the
ENTIRE cgame subsystem — 47 functions across **784 wasted anchors** (CG_Init,
CG_Draw2D, CG_PredictPlayerState, CG_EntityEvent, CG_RegisterWeapon,
CG_RegisterDvars with 291 anchors behind it). `"Str"` likewise killed
StringTable_Lookup and String_Parse. Quantified by `re/cod4x_filtercost.py`:
786 of 3,710 usable anchors thrown away.

**Second**: I replaced the blocklist with regexes and put `SC[A-Z]` in for Apple's
SystemConfiguration — which matches **SCR_** (screen). `SCR_StopCinematic` and
`SCR_UpdateFrame` were rejected exactly as CG_ had been. **The AUDIT caught this
one**, as a phantom-reference finding, which is the whole reason check D exists.

THE ACTUAL DISCRIMINATOR IS THE UNDERSCORE, not the letters. Every engine name is
`XX_Something` (CG_ SCR_ CL_ SV_ R_ UI_ FS_ BG_ SND_ MSG_ NET_ SEH_ DB_ FX_); no
Apple framework name has an underscore that early (CGColorRelease, NSRectFill,
IOObjectRelease, SCNetworkCheck). So `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]{0,4}_` EXEMPTS a name
from every framework pattern.

**RULE: never filter engine names by a bare letter prefix.** Two-letter prefixes
collide with subsystem names across the whole CoD codebase. And when a filter
rejects most of a reference set, PRINT WHAT IT IS REJECTING before believing the
result — that diagnostic is what found this both times.

## ⭐ THE PRINCIPLED REPLACEMENT — SEGMENT EVIDENCE, NOT NAME GUESSING

macOS system APIs are Mach-O IMPORT STUBS. Measured: `_atoi`, `_glFogi`,
`_CFArrayGetTypeID` all live in **__symbol_stub** (737 of them), while real engine
bodies — `Sys_Init`, `FS_FileSeek`, and statically-linked ODE like `dMessage` —
live in **__text** (8,402). `re/xsegs.py` dumps the bounds; `is_import_stub(ea)`
is a checkable test that replaces most of the guesswork. ODE and libjpeg are now
correctly ALLOWED, because they really are linked into both builds.

## ⭐⭐ THE FIX'S PAYOFF, AND A LARGE INDEPENDENT VALIDATION

    usable anchors        2,924 -> 3,710
    AGREE with an already-applied name   478
    CONFLICT with an already-applied name  0

**478 functions where a string anchor and independent call-graph propagation
agree, and NOT ONE disagreement.** That is the strongest single validation in
either CoD4X pass. CG_ is now the largest named prefix in the binary:

    CG(60) SV(58) CL(57) Com(57) Scr(56) R(56) G(38) UI(36) GScr(33) PC(28)
    FS(24) Dvar(21) BG(17) SEH(14) Sys(13) DB(11) FX(11) NET(11) MSG(11)

## ⭐ THE REUSABLE EVALUATION HARNESS — build this before any new method

`re/cod4x_evaluate.py`. Given a proposals file, it reports agreement against
functions already named by independent means, so a method is MEASURED before it
is trusted. It REFUSES to be used as a basis when the overlap is under 20.

`--truth=<regex>` restricts ground truth by basis comment. That matters: measuring
a GRAPH method against names graph propagation produced is self-agreement, not a
measurement. Every graph result below is measured against STRING-derived names
only.

## FOUR NEW METHODS. TWO WORKED, TWO ARE MEASURED NEGATIVES.

### ✅ string-SET similarity, mutual-best  (re/cod4x_strsets.py) -> +63

Anchors need a string owned by exactly ONE function on BOTH sides. This instead
scores whole string SETS, `shared / min(|R|,|T|)`, and accepts only MUTUALLY BEST
pairs with a margin over each side's runner-up. Mutual-best plus margin is what
stops a big dispatcher absorbing every function it shares one string with.

Swept, and the sweep is the point:

    min_shared min_score margin  precision   new
        1        0.25     1.0     95.17%     179
        1        0.25     1.2     99.47%      25
        2        0.25     1.0     98.10%      84   <- chosen
        2        0.25     1.5    100.00%       9

### ✅ dominance-weighted graph vote  (re/cod4x_vote.py) -> +41 (+24 in the loop)

`cod4x_propagate.py` demands the neighbour intersection leave EXACTLY ONE
survivor; one inlined call edge empties it. Here neighbours VOTE, weighted by
RARITY (`1/log2(2+callers-1)`), so being called by a 3-caller function counts for
far more than being called by Com_Printf — that weighting is what stops hubs
dominating every ballot.

5-fold cross-validated against STRING-derived names only:

    min_votes ratio  recovered  precision
      2.0     2.0        21     100.00%
      1.5     1.5        55     100.00%
      1.0     1.3        91      98.90%   <- chosen
    the single error: Scr_AddFields vs Scr_AddFields_FastFile (near-twins)

### ⛔ constant-set matching  (re/cod4x_constants.py) — NOT APPLIED

Reaches functions with NO strings, which is the right target population. Extracts
integer immediates (excluding anything address-like, since addresses differ
between builds) and float/double literals reached by data refs.

    min_shared/score/margin   overlap  precision  new
        3 / 0.5 / 1.2            2      100.00%    12
        2 / 0.4 / 1.2           10       80.00%    24
        2 / 0.3 / 1.0           14       78.57%    42

At thresholds loose enough to measure, precision is ~79% — far below the ~98%
standard. Constants here are too low-entropy: only ~2,800 distinct tokens across
~3,900 functions. **The applier's "refuse if overlap < 20" guard blocked it
automatically**, which is exactly what that guard is for. Not applied.

### ⛔ global / data cross-reference matching  (re/cod4x_globals.py) — NOT APPLIED

Two stages: vote (target_global, reference_global) over already-trusted function
pairs, then match unnamed functions by their translated global sets. It would also
have given us DATA names, of which we have none.

STARVED BY A STRUCTURAL LIMIT, not by tuning: **only 2,733 of 9,140 reference
functions have ANY direct global reference**, because GCC's i386 Mach-O accesses
globals through PIC indirection. 1,732 of 1,835 global candidates fell below
support. At loose settings: 88 globals mapped, 15 function proposals, no
measurable overlap. Not applied.

⭐ WORTH KEEPING: the small mapping it does produce is **offset-preserving** —
`0x1cbfc84 -> 0x463804` (support 13) and `0x1cbfc8c -> 0x46380c` (support 7),
8 bytes apart on BOTH sides, voted independently. So the idea is sound and would
work against a non-PIC reference; it is the reference build that cannot feed it.

## ⭐⭐⭐ THE REAL CEILING IS MAPPING DENSITY, NOT METHOD CLEVERNESS

The voting run's own statistics name the bottleneck:

    too_little_support   7,567     <- fewer than 2 MAPPED neighbours
    skipped_hub          1,189
    below_min_votes        489

Most unnamed functions have no mapped neighbour at all, so no graph method can
reach them however it is tuned. Every name that lands raises the density and
unlocks neighbours for all the other methods — the methods are not alternatives,
they are a RATCHET.

`re/cod4x_megaloop.py` runs all three working methods in one loop, refreshing the
graph from the IDB each round and merging in order of MEASURED precision:

    round 1: 1,461 -> +17   (graph 3, strset 0, vote 14)
    round 2: 1,478 -> +6
    round 3: 1,484 -> +1
    round 4: converged

Nothing is loosened; the gain is purely density. **Re-run the megaloop after ANY
future naming work** — it is free and it compounds.

## ⛔ A CLEANUP THAT DAMAGED THE IDB, AND HOW IT WAS CAUGHT

`ida_name.set_name(..., SN_FORCE)` **does not fail on a name collision — it
appends `_0` and reports success.** So a duplicate proposal became
`CL_InitOnceForAllClients_0`, a name in NEITHER binary. The audit flagged it as a
phantom.

My fix then reverted every `base_N` name whose base was in use — and swept up **22
PRE-EXISTING IDA names** that had nothing to do with this pass: `start_0`..
`start_15` (IDA's own numbering of CRT entry thunks) and `__alloca_probe_8` /
`__alloca_probe_16` / `_copy_environ_0` / `__mkgmtime_0`, which are REAL and
DISTINCT MSVC CRT symbols. All 22 were restored from the pre-change dump by
`re/cod4x_restore_dupes.py`; only the one function this pass had actually named
stayed reverted to `sub_`, with a comment saying the evidence pointed at either it
or the function holding the base name, unresolved.

**TWO RULES FROM THIS:**
  * after `set_name`, READ THE NAME BACK and compare. SN_FORCE mangles silently.
  * a cleanup that edits by NAME PATTERN must also check PROVENANCE. Only touch
    what this pass wrote — the `Basis:` comment is what makes that possible, which
    is a second reason the mandatory-basis rule pays off.

    xconsts.py             per-function literal-constant sets
    xdrefs.py              per-function referenced-global sets
    mutualbest.py          generic mutual-best feature-set matcher (shared core)
    cod4x_filtercost.py    what a name filter actually COSTS, in lost names
    cod4x_evaluate.py      MEASURE any method; --truth avoids circular validation
    cod4x_rescore.py       re-score and classify NEW / AGREE / CONFLICT

## WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT, now that the ceiling is understood

  1. **Density is the constraint.** Anything that maps even a few hundred more
     functions unlocks the graph methods across the rest. The best untried source
     is CoD4X's own structure, not the reference: vtables/RTTI (`??0exception@std@@`
     shows MSVC RTTI is present), switch-table shapes, and the 47 ambiguous
     Mac-inlined/CoD4X-split families.
  2. **A non-PIC reference would make the global method work**, and it is already
     written. Any other CoD4 build with direct global addressing feeds it.
  3. CoD4X's own additions (its `goprone` is already named) cannot come from a
     2007 reference at all and need target-only evidence.

# CoD4X PASS 3 — ADDRESS ORDER (dead), AMBIGUOUS ANCHORS, AND THE ENSEMBLE TIER
# 2026-08-17, same session.  1,487 -> 1,498 named.  Audit PASS. IDB saved.

Small numeric gain, but it establishes a NEW EVIDENCE TIER that should be reached
for first in any future pass, and it kills one idea permanently.

## ⛔ MEASURED NEGATIVE — ADDRESS ORDER IS NOT PRESERVED. Do not build on it.

Both binaries are built from the same sources, and compilers emit functions in
source order within a translation unit, so bracketing two matched functions and
aligning what lies between LOOKS like free names. Measured first
(`re/cod4x_ordercheck.py`), over 912 trusted pairs sorted by reference address:

    consecutive pairs where the TARGET address also increases:
        494 / 911 = 54.2%          (50% is chance - so there is no global signal)
    monotone runs: 418, longest 12, runs of >=5 cover only 22.4% of pairs
    brackets with matching function counts on both sides: 11 of 315

The local runs are real (order IS preserved inside a translation unit) but the
LINK order of translation units differs completely, so a global address alignment
is worthless here. 95,002 unnamed target functions fall inside the brackets,
which is a measure of how meaningless the brackets are.

**Do not revisit address/locality alignment for this pair.** It is also exactly
the "mapped by position" evidence this project has been burned by before
(sub_9192E0), so the bar for it was always going to be high.

## ⭐ NEW METHOD — CONSTRAINT DEDUCTION ON AMBIGUOUS ANCHORS

The anchor pass discards any string with 2+ owners on either side (648 reference,
44 target). Ambiguity is not uselessness: if a string is owned by {r1,r2} and
{t1,t2} and r1 is already known to be t1, then **r2 must be t2**. Deduction, not
guessing. Generalised: drop the already-mapped members from both owner sets; if
exactly one candidate remains on each side, the pair is forced.

    153 forced deductions -> 44 proposals, 0 contradicted by another string

But cross-validated (hide known names, rebuild the mapping, re-derive) it scores
**96.47% (82/85)** - below the ~98% bar the other applied methods cleared.

Tightening did NOT help, and that is the diagnostic:

    ">=1 anchor in common"  -> 96.77%
    strict set correspondence -> 96.47%
    strict + >=2 witnesses    -> 91.18%   (WORSE)

The same three errors survive every tightening and even GAIN witnesses, so they
are systematically wrong rather than thinly supported. Not applied on its own.

## ⭐⭐⭐ THE ENSEMBLE TIER — REQUIRE TWO METHODS THAT SHARE NO EVIDENCE TO AGREE

Instead of loosening the bar to ship the deduction, require CORROBORATION: accept
a deduced pair only when the call-graph weighted vote independently ranks the
SAME reference function top for that target. One method uses string ownership,
the other call-graph topology; they share no evidence.

    deduction alone            96.47%  (82/85)
    deduction + graph agreement  100.00%  (53/53)   <- every error removed

That is the strongest tier reached in this project short of self-naming, and it
cost one small script (`re/cod4x_ensemble.py`). **Reach for ensemble agreement
before loosening any threshold.**

⚠ The three errors it removes are worth a second look by anyone continuing: by
address neighbourhood the DEDUCTION looks more plausible than the name currently
applied, e.g. 0x55e140 sits beside FS_Startup (0x55e390) and the deduction says
FS_RemoveCommands while the graph vote had said Dvar_SetBool; 0x46d4e0 sits in the
CL_ cluster and the deduction says CL_InitDedicated. Recorded as open
contradictions, not resolved.

## Final state of the CoD4X pass

    applied this session: 925, every one with a recorded basis
    audit PASS - 0 duplicates, 0 phantom references, 0 contradictions-with-source

    by method:  anchors 480 | propagation 305 | vote 66 | strset 63
                ensemble 8  | cmdtable 2 | self-naming 1

## Tooling added in pass 3

`cod4x_apply_method.py` gained `--measured`, because a method that only proposes
for UNNAMED functions can never be scored by overlap and must carry its own

## ⚠ TWO PROCESS TRAPS HIT AGAIN IN THIS PASS

  * **module-level argv parsing fires on IMPORT.** `cod4x_ensemble.py` imports
    `cod4x_ambiguous`, whose `--crossval` branch then ran and `sys.exit(0)`d,
    so the ensemble printed the WRONG method's numbers. Guard every script body
    with `if __name__ == "__main__":`. (Same trap as cod4x_propagate.py earlier.)
  * **a str.replace patch that does not match fails SILENTLY.** The `--measured`
    patch appeared to succeed ("patched" printed) and had done nothing; only
    grepping the file showed it. Assert the pattern matched, or use the editor.

# ⭐⭐⭐ CoD4 READER — THE THREE DEFECTS FIXED, AND ONE NEW ONE EXPOSED (2026-08-17)

## PROVEN — all 16 CoD4 netfield tables, dumped BY POINTER with the binary's own counts

`re/dump_cod4_all.py` -> `re/cod4_all_netfields.json`, and the reader's copies in
`demo-corpus/docs/cod4_to_h1/iw3_<table>.json`.

Counts are read from the binary (`s_netFieldList` entries, and the `_num*Fields`
symbols for the standalone tables), never from a name-scan terminator — which is
what previously reported clientStateFields as 165 instead of 24.

    entityStateFields 59      playerEntityStateFields 59   corpseEntityStateFields 59
    itemEntityStateFields 59  missileEntityStateFields 59  scriptMoverStateFields 59
    soundBlendEntityStateFields 59  fxStateFields 59       loopFxEntityStateFields 59
    helicopterEntityStateFields 58  planeStateFields 60    vehicleEntityStateFields 59
    eventEntityStateFields 59
    clientStateFields 24      playerStateFields 141        objectiveFields 6

## ⭐ PROVEN — the eType dispatch, from `s_netFieldList` @0x410040

`MSG_GetStateFieldListForEntityType` is `return &s_netFieldList + 2*min(eType,17)`
over an 18-entry `{NetField*, count}` array. It CLAMPS rather than bounds-checks.

    0 ET_GENERAL        entityStateFields        9  ET_LOOP_FX        loopFxEntityStateFields
    1 ET_PLAYER         playerEntityStateFields 10  ET_PRIMARY_LIGHT  entityStateFields
    2 ET_PLAYER_CORPSE  corpseEntityStateFields 11  ET_TURRET         entityStateFields
    3 ET_ITEM           itemEntityStateFields   12  ET_HELICOPTER     helicopterEntityStateFields
    4 ET_MISSILE        missileEntityStateFields 13 ET_PLANE          planeStateFields
    5 ET_INVISIBLE      entityStateFields       14  ET_VEHICLE        vehicleEntityStateFields
    6 ET_SCRIPTMOVER    scriptMoverStateFields  15  ET_VEHICLE_COLLMAP entityStateFields
    7 ET_SOUND_BLEND    soundBlendEntityStateFields 16 ET_VEHICLE_CORPSE entityStateFields
    8 ET_FX             fxStateFields           17  ET_EVENTS         eventEntityStateFields

`ET_EVENTS(17) -> eventEntityStateFields` is where the EV_OBITUARY temp entity
lands, so the killfeed depends on this dispatch being right.

And `MSG_ReadDeltaEntity` confirms the TWO-STAGE read from its own decompile:

    MSG_ReadDeltaField(msg, t, from, to, &entityStateFields, 0)   // field[0] = eType
    fields = MSG_GetStateFieldListForEntityType(to->eType)        // THEN dispatch
    for i in 1..lc-1: MSG_ReadDeltaField(..., fields[i])

Because the ENCODERS differ between tables, using one flat table does not merely
mislabel fields — it desynchronises the BITSTREAM, so one wrong entity corrupts
every entity after it in the same packet.

## ⭐⭐ PROVEN — the CLIENT loop is structurally DIFFERENT from the entity loop

From `CL_ParseSnapshot` @0xc4e50 (the CL_ParsePacketClients section):

    while (MSG_ReadBit(msg))                 // a CONTINUE BIT per entry...
    {
        idx = MSG_ReadEntityIndex(msg, 6);   // ...and a 6-BIT index
        MSG_ReadDeltaClient(msg, time, from, to, idx);
    }

vs the entity loop's `idx = MSG_ReadEntityIndex(msg, 10); if (idx == 1023) break;`.

**The 6-bit client index IS CoD4's 64-player cap, on the wire.** `clientState_s`
is 100 bytes (0x64); `entityState_s` is 244 (0xF4).

`MSG_ReadDeltaClient` @0x17cc20 -> `MSG_ReadDeltaStruct(msg, time, from, to, idx,
24, 6, &clientStateFields, 24)`. The `6` is the lastChangedField WIDTH, taken from
the push order at 0x17cc52..0x17cc7a — a hardcoded 6 bits, the same as entities,
NOT `ceil_log2(numFields)`. (playerState's width IS computed, because 141 needs 8.)

## ⭐ clientStateFields IS THE ROSTER THE USER ASKED FOR

    modelindex(9b)  <- THE UNIFORM        team(2b)  <- THE FACTION
    name[0]/[4]/[8]/[12]  = one 16-byte char array at offset 60
    rank  prestige  perks  maxSprintTimeMultiplier
    attachModelIndex[0..5]  attachTagIndex[0..5]  attachedVehEntNum  attachedVehSlotIndex

So "uniform by faction AND by weapon class" is `team` + `modelindex` — both
replicated per client, both now readable. That question is answered at the data
level; what remains is the CoD4 modelindex -> MWR model NAME mapping table.

## THE THREE READER DEFECTS — FIXED, AND THE GAIN IS MEASURED

`tools/cod4_to_h1/iw3/{netfields,snapshot}.py`:

  1. **one flat entity table** -> two-stage per-eType dispatch (`etype_tables`,
     applied at all three call sites incl. the svc_baseline path)
  2. **`except: entities = []`** discarded EVERY correctly-decoded entity on one
     bad one -> per-entity isolation: a desync stops the loop but KEEPS what was
     already read, and sets `entities_truncated` + a `entity_desyncs` stat
  3. **client section never parsed** -> `read_delta_client` + `client_summary`,
     with the continue-bit/6-bit-index shape above

MEASURED on `demo0000.dm_1` (mp_crash, sv_maxclients=50):

    entities decoded   0  ->  4,624
    client records     0  ->  4
    snapshots decoded  2,057 / 2,491   (unchanged - not what these fixes touch)

## ⛔ NEW DEFECT, NOW VISIBLE — a PLAYERSTATE desync truncates 99.7% of entity reads

    2,050 of 2,057 decoded snapshots hit `entities_truncated`
    playerstate origin reads [0.0, 0.0, 5.557e+26]  <- garbage

`origin[0..2]` are fields 4/5/12, encoder **-88 (float32-XOR)**. A garbage value at
field 12 with 0.0 at 4/5 means the bitstream is already out of phase INSIDE the
playerstate, and the entity loop is simply the first place it becomes visible.
`lc_bits = ceil_log2(141) = 8` is correct, so the width is not the cause.

This was NOT introduced by these fixes and is not exposed by them either — it was
always there, hidden behind `entities = []`, which is precisely why removing that
blanket catch was worth doing. **This is now the top item: the POV pose and every
entity in the packet are downstream of it.**

## ⛔ CORRECTED — the old dumps' `type` field was never a field

`iw3_playerstate_netfields.json` carries `"type": 65535` on nearly every entry.
That is the HIGH HALF of a 32-bit signed `bits` (-97 = 0xFFFFFF9F), mis-split by an
earlier dump that assumed `{name, offset, i16 bits, u16 type, u32 flags}`.

The real layout is **`{const char* name; i32 offset; i32 bits; i32 changeHints}`**,
16 bytes. `read_delta_field` never reads `type`, so nothing depended on it — and the
regenerated tables are byte-identical to the old ones on every field that matters
(verified: 0 differences across playerState and entityState on
name/offset/bits/flags). So the 0 -> 4,624 entity gain is attributable purely to the
dispatch and isolation fixes, not to a table change.

## NEXT

  1. the playerstate desync (above) - blocks the pose AND the entities
  2. CoD4 modelindex -> MWR model name, and team -> MWR faction
  3. still open from before: the illegal-opcode MWR message class, weapon name ->
     MWR packed id, the Type-B `.dm_1` container
